title: Chapter 12. Of Religion
paragraphs: Since no signs or fruits of religion appear anywhere but in man, there is no reason to doubt that the seed of religion, too, is found only in man — and that it consists in some peculiar quality, or at least some outstanding degree of a quality, that is not found in other living creatures.

First, it is part of human nature — more in some people, less in others, but in everyone to some degree — to be curious about the causes of the events one sees, so that every person takes an interest in tracking down the causes of their own good and bad fortune.
Second, on seeing anything that has a beginning, a person also tends to think it had a cause that fixed it to begin exactly when it did, rather than sooner or later.

Third: animals have no happiness beyond the enjoyment of their daily food, ease, and appetites, since they have little or no foresight of the future — lacking the observation and memory needed to track the order, sequence, and dependence of the things they see. Man, by contrast, notices how one event has produced another, and remembers, in such cases, what came before and what followed. And when he cannot be certain of the true causes of things — since the causes of good and bad fortune are for the most part invisible — he supplies causes of his own: either ones his own imagination suggests, or ones he takes on the authority of other people he considers his friends and wiser than himself.

[The natural cause of religion: anxiety about the future.] The first two of these tendencies together produce anxiety. For once a person is convinced that everything that has happened, or will happen, has a cause, it becomes impossible for him — continually trying as he is to guard against the evils he fears and secure the goods he desires — not to live in a constant state of worry about the future. So every man, and especially the overly cautious ones, is in a condition much like that of Prometheus. Prometheus — whose name, translated, means "the prudent man" — was chained to Mount Caucasus, a place with a wide view over the land, where an eagle feeding on his liver ate by day exactly as much as grew back by night. In the same way, the man who looks too far ahead in his concern for the future has his heart gnawed at all day long by the fear of death, poverty, or some other disaster, and finds no rest from his anxiety except in sleep.

This constant fear, which accompanies mankind everywhere in its ignorance of causes — as if groping in the dark — must have some object. And so, when there is nothing visible to blame, people credit their good or bad fortune to some invisible power or agent instead. It may have been in this sense that some of the ancient poets said the gods were first created by human fear — which, said of the gods (that is, of the many gods of the pagans), is very true. But acknowledging one God, eternal, infinite, and all-powerful, can more readily be traced to people's desire to understand the causes of natural things and their various powers and workings, than to fear of what the future might bring. For anyone who reasons from an effect he observes back to its immediate cause, and from that cause to the cause behind it, and keeps pressing further into the chain of causes, will eventually arrive — as even the pagan philosophers admitted — at the conclusion that there must be one First Mover: that is, a first and eternal cause of everything, which is what people mean by the name "God." And all this happens without any thought of one's own fortune, since worry about fortune both breeds fear and keeps people from investigating the causes of other things — and so gives rise to as many invented gods as there are people inventing them.

As for what these imagined invisible agents were made of, natural reflection could lead people to only one idea: that they were the same kind of thing as the human soul, and that the soul itself was made of the same stuff as what appears in a dream to a sleeping person, or in a mirror to a waking one. Not knowing that such appearances are nothing but products of the imagination, people took them to be real, external beings, and so called them ghosts — as the Romans called them Imagines and Umbrae — and believed them to be spirits, that is, thin, airy bodies; and supposed the invisible agents they feared to be of the same kind, except that these could appear and vanish at will. But the idea that such spirits were incorporeal, or immaterial, could never occur naturally to any human mind — for although people can string together words that contradict each other, like "spirit" and "incorporeal," they can never form any mental picture that corresponds to them. This is why people who, through their own reasoning, arrive at acknowledging one infinite, all-powerful, eternal God prefer to admit that he is incomprehensible and beyond their understanding, rather than define his nature as "incorporeal spirit" and then have to admit that their own definition makes no sense. And if they do apply such a term to him, it is not meant literally, as an attempt to make God's nature understandable, but reverently, to honor him with descriptions as far removed as possible from the coarseness of visible bodies.

As for how people imagined these invisible agents brought about their effects — that is, what immediate causes they used to make things happen — people who do not understand what we mean by "causing" (which is to say, nearly everyone) have no way to guess except by noticing and remembering what they have seen precede a similar effect on some earlier occasion, without perceiving any actual connection or dependence between the earlier event and the one that followed. And so, from things that happened before, they expect similar things to happen again, and superstitiously hope for good or bad luck from things that had no real part in causing it at all — as when the Athenians, for their war at Lepanto, called for another Phormio, or the Pompeian faction, for their war in Africa, called for another Scipio, and as others have done on many similar occasions since. In the same way, people credit their fortune to a bystander, to a lucky or unlucky place, or to words spoken — especially if God's name is among them, as in charms and conjuring (the liturgy of witches) — to the point of believing they have the power to turn a stone into bread, bread into a man, or anything into anything.

Third, as for the worship that people naturally offer to invisible powers, it can be nothing other than the same expressions of respect they would use toward other men: gifts, requests, thanks, bowing of the body, careful speech, restrained behavior, deliberate words, and oaths — that is, calling on these powers to guarantee promises made to one another. Beyond this, reason has nothing further to suggest; it either leaves people content with these gestures, or, for any further ceremony, leaves them to rely on those they consider wiser than themselves.

Finally, as for how these invisible powers reveal to people what is going to happen — especially concerning their good or bad fortune in general, or the success or failure of some particular undertaking — people are naturally at a loss. Except that, being used to judging the future by the past, they are quick not only to treat chance occurrences, after one or two repetitions, as reliable signs of what will happen every time afterward, but also to accept similar predictions from other people they have come to think well of.

And in these four things — belief in ghosts, ignorance of secondary causes, devotion toward whatever people fear, and the treatment of chance events as omens — lies the natural seed of religion. Because people's imaginations, judgments, and passions differ so much from one person to the next, this seed has grown into ceremonies so varied that the ones practiced by one man strike another, for the most part, as ridiculous.

These seeds have been cultivated by two kinds of people. One kind has nourished and shaped them according to their own invention; the other has done so at God's own command and direction. But both kinds have done it with the same aim: to make the people who relied on them more inclined toward obedience, law, peace, charity, and civil society. So the religion of the first kind is a branch of human politics, teaching part of what earthly kings require of their subjects; and the religion of the second kind is divine politics, containing the commands given to those who have made themselves subjects of the Kingdom of God. Of the first kind were all the founders of commonwealths and the lawgivers of the pagans; of the second kind were Abraham, Moses, and our blessed Savior, through whom the laws of the Kingdom of God have come down to us.

As for that part of religion consisting in beliefs about the nature of invisible powers, there is scarcely anything with a name that has not, somewhere among the pagans, been taken for a god or a devil, or imagined by their poets to be alive, inhabited, or possessed by some spirit or other.
The unformed matter of the world was itself a god, under the name of Chaos.
The sky, the ocean, the planets, fire, the earth, the winds — all these were gods.

Men, women, a bird, a crocodile, a calf, a dog, a snake, an onion, a leek — all were deified. Beyond this, they filled almost every place with spirits called daemons: the plains with Pan and the Panises, or satyrs; the woods with fauns and nymphs; the sea with Tritons and other nymphs; every river and spring with a ghost bearing its name, and with nymphs of its own; every house with its Lares, or household spirits; every man with his own guardian genius; the underworld with ghosts and spirit officials such as Charon, Cerberus, and the Furies; and, at night, every place with Larvae, Lemures, and the ghosts of the dead, and a whole kingdom of fairies and bogeymen. They also assigned divinity, and built temples, to mere accidents and qualities — Time, Night, Day, Peace, Concord, Love, Strife, Virtue, Honor, Health, Rust, Fever, and the like — praying for or against these as if the ghosts bearing those names hovered over their heads, granting or withholding whatever good or evil was being prayed for or against. They also invoked their own cleverness under the name of the Muses; their own ignorance, under the name of Fortune; their own lust, under the name of Cupid; their own rage, under the name of the Furies; their own genitals, under the name of Priapus; and they blamed their sexual emissions on incubi and succubi — so that there was nothing a poet could bring into his poem as a character that they did not turn into either a god or a devil.

These same founders of pagan religion, noting the second root of religion — people's ignorance of causes, and their consequent readiness to credit their fortune to causes that had no visible connection to it at all — took the opportunity to fasten onto that ignorance, in place of real secondary causes, a set of subordinate, ministering gods: assigning fertility to Venus, the arts to Apollo, cunning and craft to Mercury, storms and tempests to Aeolus, and other effects to other gods — so that among the pagans there came to be almost as many gods as there were kinds of business.

And alongside the worship that people naturally felt was owed to their gods — offerings, prayers, thanks, and the other things already mentioned — these same pagan lawgivers added images of the gods, in painting and sculpture, so that the more ignorant part of the people (that is, the great majority) — believing the gods represented by these images were actually contained within them, as if housed there — would feel all the more fear of them. They endowed these images with lands, buildings, staff, and income set apart from every other human use, that is, consecrated and made holy to these idols — caves, groves, forests, mountains, even whole islands. And they gave the images not only shapes — some human, some animal, some monstrous — but also the faculties and passions of men and animals: sensation, speech, sex, lust, the capacity to reproduce (not only among themselves, to breed more gods, but also with human men and women, to produce hybrid gods who were mere lodgers in heaven, such as Bacchus and Hercules), along with anger, revenge, and the other passions of living creatures, and the actions that follow from them — fraud, theft, adultery, sodomy, and any vice that could pass either as a display of power or a source of pleasure — indeed, every vice that people consider a violation of law rather than of honor.

Finally, alongside the natural way of foretelling the future — which amounts to nothing more than guesses based on past experience — and the supernatural way, divine revelation, these same founders of pagan religion added, partly on claimed experience and partly on claimed revelation, countless other superstitious methods of divination. They led people to believe they could learn their fortunes sometimes in the ambiguous or nonsensical answers given by the priests at Delphi, Delos, Ammon, and other famous oracles — answers made deliberately vague so as to fit whatever happened afterward, or made incoherent by the intoxicating fumes common in such sulphurous caves. Sometimes they looked to the writings of the Sibyls — whose prophecies, like those perhaps of Nostradamus (the surviving fragments look like the invention of a later age), were held in some repute during the time of the Roman Republic. Sometimes they looked to the meaningless utterances of madmen, thought to be possessed by a divine spirit — a possession they called Enthusiasm, this kind of prediction being counted as Theomancy, or prophecy; to the position of the stars at a person's birth, called horoscopy and treated as a branch of judicial astrology; to a person's own hopes and fears, called Thumomancy, or foreboding; or to the claims of witches who professed to consult the dead, which is called necromancy, conjuring, and witchcraft, and is nothing but trickery and organized fraud. And sometimes they looked to the chance flight or feeding patterns of birds, called augury; to the entrails of a sacrificed animal, called Aruspicina; to dreams; to the croaking of ravens or the chattering of birds; to the features of a person's face, called Metoposcopy, or to palm-reading the lines of the hand; to chance remarks, called omens; to monstrous or unusual occurrences — eclipses, comets, rare meteors, earthquakes, floods, strange births, and the like — which they called Portenta and Ostenta, because they believed these things foretold some great disaster to come; and sometimes to pure lottery, such as Cross and Pile — that is, heads or tails — counting holes in a sieve, or opening Homer or Virgil at random and reading whatever line the eye fell on — along with countless other empty superstitions of the same kind. So easily are people led to believe anything, by anyone who has already won their trust and who can, with a light and skillful touch, take hold of their fear and their ignorance.

[The designs of the authors of the religion of the heathen.] And so the earliest founders and lawgivers of commonwealths among the pagans, whose whole purpose was simply to keep the people obedient and at peace, everywhere took pains, first, to plant in people's minds the belief that the religious precepts they handed down did not originate with themselves, but with the pronouncements of some god or other spirit — or else that they themselves were of a higher order than ordinary mortals — so that their laws would be more readily accepted. This is why Numa Pompilius claimed to have received the ceremonies he established among the Romans from the nymph Egeria; why the first king and founder of the kingdom of Peru claimed that he and his wife were children of the Sun; and why Muhammad, in setting up his new religion, claimed to have had conversations with the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. Second, they took care to make people believe that whatever the laws forbade was also displeasing to the gods. Third, they prescribed ceremonies, prayers, sacrifices, and festivals meant to appease the gods' anger — teaching that defeat in war, major epidemics, earthquakes, and each person's private misfortunes came from the anger of the gods, and that anger, in turn, came from neglecting their worship, or from forgetting or getting some point of the required ceremonies wrong. And although the ancient Romans were free to deny what the poets wrote about pain and pleasure after death — and prominent, respected figures in that society openly mocked such ideas in their public speeches — the belief in them was nevertheless always encouraged more than its denial.

Through these and similar institutions, they achieved their goal — the peace of the commonwealth — because the common people, when misfortune struck, tended to blame it on some neglect or error in their ceremonies, or on their own disobedience to the laws, and so were less inclined to rise up against their rulers. And since they were kept entertained by the spectacle and festivity of games and celebrations held in honor of the gods, they needed nothing else but bread to keep them from discontent, grumbling, and revolt against the state. This is why the Romans, who had conquered most of the known world, saw no difficulty in tolerating any religion whatsoever within the city of Rome itself, unless it contained something incompatible with their civil government. Nor do we find that any religion was banned there except that of the Jews, who — being God's own particular kingdom — considered it unlawful to acknowledge submission to any mortal king or state whatsoever. And this is how the religion of the pagans functioned as a part of their statecraft.

[The true religion, and the laws of God's kingdom, are the same.] But where God himself, through supernatural revelation, established religion, he also established for himself a particular kingdom, giving laws that governed not only how people should behave toward him but also toward one another. As a result, within the Kingdom of God, civil government and law are themselves a part of religion, and the distinction between temporal and spiritual authority has no place there. It is true that God is king of the whole earth, yet he may also be king of one particular, chosen nation — there is no more contradiction in this than in the fact that the general who commands an entire army may also have his own personal regiment or company. God is king of the whole earth by his power, but of his chosen people he is king by covenant. I have set aside a later place in this work to discuss the Kingdom of God more fully, both by nature and by covenant.

From how religion spreads, it is not hard to grasp how it also breaks back down into its original seeds or principles — which amount to nothing more than a belief in a deity and in invisible, supernatural powers. These beliefs can never be so thoroughly stamped out of human nature that new religions cannot spring from them again, cultivated by whoever happens to hold the standing needed for the purpose.

For every organized religion is founded, at the start, on the trust a large number of people place in a single person — someone they believe to be not only wise and working for their happiness, but also holy, someone to whom God himself chooses to reveal his will directly. It necessarily follows that once those who administer religion come under suspicion for their wisdom, their sincerity, or their goodwill, or once they can no longer produce any convincing sign of divine revelation, the religion they wish to maintain will likewise come under suspicion — and, wherever the civil authorities do not enforce it by fear, it will be contradicted and cast aside.

What destroys the reputation for wisdom of someone who founds a religion, or adds to one already founded, is requiring people to believe contradictions. Both halves of a contradiction cannot possibly be true, so demanding belief in both is a mark of ignorance — one that exposes the person responsible in that instance, and undermines confidence in everything else he claims to have received by supernatural revelation. A person may indeed receive revelation of many things beyond natural reason, but never of anything opposed to it.

What destroys the reputation for sincerity is doing or saying things that look like signs that the person does not actually believe what he requires others to believe. Such acts and statements are called scandalous, because they are stumbling blocks that trip people up on the path of religion — things like injustice, cruelty, irreverence, greed, and self-indulgence. For who can believe that a person who habitually does the kinds of things that spring from these vices really believes in the same invisible power he uses to terrify other people over far smaller faults?

What destroys the reputation for goodwill is being caught pursuing private interests — as when the beliefs demanded of others happen to serve, or appear to serve, the acquisition of power, wealth, status, or comfortable pleasure for the person requiring belief, alone or especially. For whatever benefits people reap for themselves, they are assumed to be pursuing for their own sake, not out of love for others.

Finally, the only proof anyone can offer of a divine calling is the performance of miracles, or true prophecy (which is itself a kind of miracle), or extraordinary good fortune. And so, beyond the articles of religion received from people who performed such miracles, any further articles added by people who cannot back their own calling with a miracle gain no more belief than whatever the customs and laws of the place where people were raised have already instilled in them. For just as in ordinary matters, sensible people demand natural evidence and arguments, so in supernatural matters they demand supernatural evidence — that is, miracles — before they will genuinely believe, from the heart.

All these causes of the weakening of people's faith show up plainly in the examples that follow. First there is the example of the children of Israel, who — when Moses, who had proven his calling to them through miracles and by successfully leading them out of Egypt, was gone for only forty days — abandoned the worship of the true God he had taught them, and, setting up (Exodus 32:1–2) a golden calf as their god, fell back into the idol-worship of the Egyptians from whom they had so recently been freed. And again, after Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and the whole generation that had witnessed God's great works in Israel had died (Judges 2:11), a new generation arose and served Baal. So that when miracles stopped, faith failed along with them.

Again, when the sons of Samuel (1 Samuel 8:3), whom their father had made judges in Beersheba, took bribes and judged unfairly, the people of Israel refused to go on having God as their king in any way different from how other nations had kings, and so demanded that Samuel choose them a king like the other nations had. So that when justice failed, faith failed along with it — to the point that they deposed their own God from ruling over them.

And when Christianity took root, the oracles fell silent throughout the Roman Empire, and the number of Christians grew astonishingly, day by day and place by place, through the preaching of the apostles and evangelists. A good part of that success can reasonably be credited to the contempt the pagan priests of that era had brought upon themselves through their impurity, greed, and playing rulers against one another. In much the same way, the religion of the Church of Rome was, in part for the same reason, abolished in England and many other parts of Christendom — so that a failure of virtue among the clergy leads directly to a failure of faith among the people — and in part because of the way the schoolmen — that is, the scholastic theologians — brought Aristotle's philosophy and doctrine into religion, giving rise to so many contradictions and absurdities that the clergy earned a reputation for both ignorance and dishonest intent, driving people to break away from them, whether against the wishes of their own rulers, as in France and Holland, or with their rulers' backing, as in England.

Finally, among the articles the Church of Rome declares necessary for salvation, there are so many that plainly benefit the Pope and his spiritual subjects living within the territories of other Christian rulers, that if it weren't for the rivalry among those rulers, they could exclude all foreign authority without war or trouble, just as easily as it has already been excluded in England. For who fails to see whose interest is served by getting people to believe: that a king has no authority from Christ unless a bishop crowns him? That a king who is also a priest cannot marry? That whether a prince was born within a lawful marriage must be judged by authority from Rome? That subjects may be released from their loyalty if the Court of Rome declares the king a heretic? That a king — like Chilperic of France — may be deposed by a pope — like Pope Zachary — for no cause at all, and his kingdom handed to one of his own subjects? That the clergy and members of religious orders, in whatever country they live, should be exempt from their king's jurisdiction in criminal matters? Or who fails to see who profits from the fees charged for private Masses, and from payments made to shorten time in Purgatory, along with other unmistakable marks of private interest — enough to mortify even the most lively faith, if, as I have said, civil authority and custom did not sustain it far more than any real belief people hold in the holiness, wisdom, or integrity of their teachers? So that I can trace every change of religion the world has seen back to one and the same cause: priests who make themselves disliked — and this holds not only among Catholics, but even within the church that has claimed the most credit for reforming itself.
